Exempt vs Non-Exempt: The Three Tests That Decide Your Overtime Pay

Direct AnswerExempt vs non-exempt: salary alone doesn't decide it. The 2026 federal floor is $684 a week, plus salary-basis and duties tests. Who gets overtime, explained.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published October 24, 2026•10 min read•Overtime & Paycheck Guides

Quick Answer

Being paid a salary does not make you exempt from overtime — you must pass all three FLSA tests: salary basis, at least $684 a week, and qualifying executive, administrative, or professional duties.

Being paid a salary does not make you exempt from overtime. Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, an employee is exempt only if they pass three tests at once: they are paid on a salary basis, they earn at least $684 a week, and their actual duties fit an executive, administrative, or professional exemption. Fail any one test and overtime is owed — no matter what the job title says, and no matter how the offer letter describes the role.

This distinction decides real money. A non-exempt employee working 50 hours earns overtime for the 10 hours beyond 40; an exempt employee working the same 50 hours earns exactly the same salary as a 40-hour week. The sections below explain each test, the salary rule that was announced, vacated, and then formally withdrawn, and the worked examples that show which side of the line you fall on.

The Short Answer: Three Tests, Not One Title

Employers sometimes treat a salary or a "manager" title as proof of exempt status. The law does neither. The three tests are cumulative — all three must be satisfied:

TestWhat It RequiresIf It Fails
Salary basisA predetermined, fixed salary that does not shrink with hours worked or outputNot a true salary — exemption fails
Salary levelAt least $684 per week ($35,568 per year)Non-exempt, regardless of duties
DutiesPrimary duty fits an executive, administrative, or professional exemptionNon-exempt, regardless of pay

A highly compensated employee shortcut also exists: total annual compensation of at least $107,432, including at least $684 a week paid on a salary or fee basis, plus office or non-manual work and at least one exempt duty performed customarily and regularly.

The Three Tests, Explained

Test 1: Salary basis

An exempt employee receives a guaranteed amount each pay period that does not vary with the number of hours worked or the quantity or quality of the work. If the employee works any part of a week, the full salary for that week is owed. The employer generally cannot dock pay for a partial-day absence. Deductions are permitted only in narrow cases: full-day absences for personal reasons, full-day absences for sickness under a bona fide sick-leave plan, unpaid leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act, and certain disciplinary suspensions. Repeated improper deductions can destroy the exemption entirely, converting the employee to non-exempt status.

Test 2: Salary level

The salary must be at least $684 per week, which is $35,568 a year or $2,964 a month for a full-year worker. For comparison, $684 a week equals $17.10 an hour on a 40-hour week and $19.54 an hour on a 35-hour week. Up to 10% of the level — $68.40 a week — may be met with nondiscretionary bonuses, incentives, or commissions paid at least annually, with a catch-up payment allowed shortly after year-end if the total falls short. Computer employees have an alternative: an hourly rate of at least $27.63. Doctors, lawyers, teachers, and outside sales employees are not subject to the salary basis or salary level tests at all.

Test 3: Duties

The employee's primary duty must genuinely fit one of the recognized exemptions. An executive manages an enterprise or a recognized department, supervises two or more full-time employees, and has real authority over hiring and firing (or suggestions that carry particular weight). An administrative employee performs office or non-manual work directly related to management or general business operations and exercises discretion and independent judgment on matters of significance. A professional performs work requiring advanced knowledge gained through prolonged specialized instruction (the learned professions), or work requiring invention, imagination, originality, or talent (the creative professions). In every case, the Department of Labor looks at what the person actually does day to day — not the title on the business card.

What Happened to the $1,128 Rule?

Readers who followed this subject in 2024 may remember a different number. In April 2024, the Department of Labor issued a final rule raising the salary level to $844 a week on July 1, 2024, and then to $1,128 a week on January 1, 2025, with further increases scheduled every three years. On November 15, 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas vacated the entire rule nationwide, finding it exceeded the Department's authority. The appeals were later dismissed, and in May 2026 the Department formally rescinded the 2024 rule and restored the 2019 levels through a technical amendment. The $844 and $1,128 figures are therefore not enforceable, and any source still quoting them as current federal law is out of date. Employers that raised salaries in 2024 to meet the higher thresholds are not required to reverse those raises — but the federal floor they must meet is $684 a week.

Exempt vs Non-Exempt, Side by Side

ExemptNon-Exempt
Pay structureFixed salary, same every weekHourly or salaried, with overtime on top
Overtime (over 40 hrs/week)None — salary does not changeAt least 1.5× the regular rate
Hours trackingUsually not trackedHours must be recorded
TaxesIncome tax, Social Security, Medicare all applySame — exemption is from overtime, not tax
Typical rolesDepartment managers, senior analysts, licensed professionalsHourly staff, and salaried staff who fail any test

One point the table makes clear: "exempt" says nothing about taxes. Both kinds of employees pay the same payroll taxes. The only thing an exemption removes is the overtime premium — which is precisely why the tests exist, and why employers cannot grant themselves an exemption by re-titling a job. Note also that federal law sets no daily overtime rule; overtime is weekly, beyond 40 hours, although some states add daily thresholds of their own.

Worked Examples: The Same Hours, Different Pay

WorkerMathResult
Non-exempt, $25/hr, 45-hour week40 × $25 + 5 × $37.50$1,187.50 (overtime premium: $62.50)
Exempt, $700/week salary, 50-hour weekFixed salary, no overtime$700 — $14.00 per hour actually worked
Salaried at $35,000/year$35,000 ÷ 52 = $673.08/weekBelow the $684 floor — non-exempt regardless of duties
Salaried at $36,400/year$36,400 ÷ 52 = $700/weekLevel passed — duties now decide

The 50-hour comparison is the sharpest illustration of the stakes: at $25 an hour, a non-exempt 50-hour week pays $1,375 (40 hours at $25 plus 10 hours at $37.50), while a $52,000 salary — the same $25 rate on paper — pays a flat $1,000 for that week. Exempt status can be worth several hundred dollars a week to the employer, which is why the duties test, not the title, controls. Common Traps and Confusions

  • "Manager" on the title. A "shift manager" who spends 80% of the shift doing the same work as the crew, with little real authority over hiring or the department, generally does not pass the executive duties test — whatever the title says.
  • Salary means exempt. Salary is how pay is delivered, not a legal classification. Salaried non-exempt employees exist in large numbers, and they are owed overtime.
  • Exempt means tax-exempt. It does not. Overtime exemption and tax withholding are unrelated; "exempt from withholding" on Form W-4 is a different status with its own conditions.
  • Meeting the federal floor is always enough. It is not, where a state sets a higher threshold. Several states — including California, New York, and Washington — require more than $684 a week for exemption, and the higher figure governs. Check the current threshold for your state before relying on the federal number.
  • Full-time means exempt. It does not. Whether a job is full-time is a separate question from whether it is exempt — our guide to how many hours a week count as full-time explains why the two labels are independent, and holiday pay follows yet another set of rules.

What To Do If You Are Misclassified

Start with three checks you can run yourself: (1) divide your annual salary by 52 — if the result is below $684 a week, the federal salary level test fails outright; (2) compare your actual daily work with the duties described above, not your title; (3) check whether your state sets a higher salary threshold than the federal floor. If any check fails, you may be owed back overtime — generally for the past two years, or three if the violation was willful, plus an equal amount as liquidated damages in many cases. Keep pay stubs and a record of hours worked. This article is general information, not legal advice; a labor attorney or the Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division can assess a specific situation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick answers to the questions readers ask most about exempt and non-exempt status.

What is the difference between exempt and non-exempt employees?

The difference is overtime rights. A non-exempt employee must be paid at least time-and-a-half for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek. An exempt employee is not entitled to overtime pay, no matter how many hours the week runs. Exempt status is decided by three tests — salary basis, salary level, and duties — and all three must be met.

Is $684 a week still the salary threshold in 2026?

Yes. The federal salary level for the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions is $684 per week ($35,568 per year). The Department of Labor tried to raise it to $844 in July 2024 and $1,128 in January 2025, but a federal court vacated that rule nationwide in November 2024, and the Department formally restored the 2019 levels in May 2026. Any article still quoting $1,128 as the current federal threshold is out of date.

If I am salaried, am I automatically exempt?

No. Salary is a method of payment; exempt is a legal status. A salaried employee who fails any of the three tests — for example, earning $673 a week, below the $684 floor, or doing work that does not meet any duties test — is non-exempt and owed overtime. Many employers keep salaried non-exempt staff on a fixed weekly salary and pay overtime on top of it.

Do exempt employees get overtime pay?

No. An exempt employee receives the same fixed salary whether the week runs 35 hours or 60. That is the real price of exempt status: a $700-a-week salary pays $700 for a 50-hour week, which works out to $14.00 an hour, while a non-exempt worker at a comparable rate would earn overtime for the 10 hours beyond 40.

Does "exempt" mean exempt from taxes?

No. Exempt here means exempt from overtime pay only. Both exempt and non-exempt employees pay federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare on their earnings. A separate concept — claiming "exempt from withholding" on Form W-4 — is about income tax withholding, not overtime, and has its own strict conditions.

What if my employer calls me exempt but I do non-exempt work?

Your duties and pay decide your status, not your title. If your actual day-to-day work does not meet any duties test, or your salary falls below the federal floor (or a higher state threshold where one applies), you may be misclassified and owed back overtime. This article is general information, not legal advice; a labor attorney or the Department of Labor can assess a specific situation.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

What to Remember

  • Three tests, all required: salary basis, salary level of at least $684 a week, and qualifying duties. Fail one and overtime is owed.
  • The current federal floor is $684 a week — the $1,128 figure from the 2024 rule was vacated in November 2024 and formally withdrawn in May 2026.
  • Titles decide nothing. A manager who mostly does crew work, or a salaried worker below $684 a week, is non-exempt.
  • Long weeks price the difference: at $25 an hour, a 50-hour week pays $1,375 non-exempt versus a flat $1,000 on a $52,000 salary.
  • States can be stricter — where a state threshold exceeds the federal floor, the higher number governs.

Sources & Method

Tests and thresholds are stated as published by the U.S. Department of Labor (FLSA regulations Part 541; the Department's overtime advisor confirms the $684-per-week salary level and the $107,432 highly compensated threshold) and the court history of the 2024 rule (vacated nationwide November 15, 2024, by the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas; appeals dismissed May 2026; 2019 levels restored by Department technical amendment effective May 15, 2026). Annual figures use 52 weeks; overtime examples use time-and-a-half over 40 hours in a workweek. This article is general information, not legal advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. Salary alone is not enough — fail any one of the three tests and overtime is owed.
  2. The salary test is at least $684 a week, paid on a salary basis.
  3. The duties test is about your actual duties fitting an executive, administrative, or professional exemption.
